title: Russia, sanctions and the price of India's balancing act
hook:
In April 2022, a few weeks after Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine, India's foreign minister S. Jaishankar stood at a press conference in Washington after talks with his American counterparts. A reporter asked why India was buying Russian oil. His answer became famous. India's purchases for a whole month, he said, were probably less than what Europe bought in an afternoon. If you are worried about Russian energy, he suggested, look at Europe.

For three years that line held. India bought discounted Russian crude by the shipload, its refiners made handsome margins, and Washington grumbled but mostly let it pass. Then in August 2025 the bill arrived: an extra penalty tariff on Indian goods, aimed squarely at those oil purchases, which roughly doubled the US duty on everything from shirts to shrimp.

India calls its foreign policy strategic autonomy: friends with everyone, allied with no one. It is a sensible strategy for a large country in a divided world. But each relationship has a market price, and sanctions are how that price gets collected. This chapter explains how the Russian discount worked, how sanctions actually bite, and which Indian stocks end up paying.
short: India keeps close ties with the US, Russia, the Gulf and, warily, China at the same time. Each partner holds a lever over India, and the US lever (tariffs and sanctions) is the one markets feel most.
Discounted Russian crude after 2022 lowered India's oil bill and helped hold down inflation, a real gain that mostly showed up in refiners' and the government's accounts.
Sanctions bite through the financial plumbing: banks, insurers and shipping, not just the oil itself. That is why the risk sits with refiners, exporters and the banks that finance trade.

In 2025 the US imposed a penalty tariff tied to Russian oil and sanctioned Russia's biggest oil companies. A February 2026 deal removed the penalty, and in mid-October 2026 the US paused a heavier new round a day before it took effect, keeping the right to bring it back.
The impact is sectoral, not systemic: refiners, exporters to the US, banks with trade-finance exposure, and defence.

sections.heading: Friends with everyone, allied with no one
sections.html:
India has never liked choosing sides. During the Cold War it led the non-aligned movement while buying most of its weapons from the Soviet Union. Since the 1990s it has grown much closer to the United States, without signing up to an alliance. Today it buys oil and gas mostly from the Gulf, sat for years as one of the largest buyers of Russian crude, sells software and medicines to America, and imports a huge share of its electronics and chemical inputs from China, the country it fought on its northern border in 2020.

Diplomats call this strategic autonomy. Investors should think of it as a portfolio of relationships, each with a return and a risk.

[[fig:1]]

The diagram lays out the four relationships that matter most and, crucially, the lever each partner holds over India. Read it from the right-hand side of each box. The United States offers technology, capital, the biggest export market and a defence partnership, and it can hurt India through tariffs, sanctions and visas. Russia offers discounted crude and keeps the old weapons running, but buying from it exposes India to American and European sanctions. The Gulf supplies most of India's oil and gas and employs millions of Indians whose remittances support the rupee; the risk there is war. China supplies the inputs for electronics, solar and pharma, and its levers are export controls and the border.

Here's the thing. These levers are not equally strong. The US lever is the one with direct, immediate market consequences, because America is India's largest export market and because the dollar runs through almost every international payment India makes. Russia can offer a discount; it cannot offer access to the world's financial system. That asymmetry explains most of what happened between 2022 and 2026.

sections.heading: How the Russian discount worked
sections.html:
Before the invasion, Russia was a minor supplier of crude to India. Its oil had to travel a long way, and Indian refiners had settled supply deals with Saudi Arabia, Iraq and the Emirates. Then Europe, Russia's biggest customer, began shutting the door. Western buyers shunned Russian cargoes, and from December 2022 the Group of Seven rich democracies imposed a price cap: Western shippers and insurers could only handle Russian oil sold below a set price.

A seller who loses his biggest customer has to cut prices to find new ones. Russia's main export grade began selling at a deep discount to the global benchmark. Indian refiners, both private ones like Reliance's giant complex at Jamnagar and Nayara Energy's refinery at Vadinar, which is part-owned by Russia's Rosneft, and the state-owned companies, stepped in. Within months Russia went from a bit player to India's single largest crude supplier.

What did India gain? Think of it as buying the same groceries from a wholesaler who badly needs cash. A cheaper average barrel shrinks the import bill, eases pressure on the rupee and keeps a lid on fuel inflation. Refiners could also turn the cheap crude into diesel and jet fuel and export it at full global prices, some of it to the very European countries that had stopped buying Russian crude directly.

The Russian discount was real money. The question was always who would send the bill, and when.

One detail matters for investors. Indian pump prices for petrol and diesel were held largely steady through this period, so ordinary drivers saw little of the discount directly. The gain showed up instead in refining margins, in state oil companies' balance sheets, and in a smaller national oil bill. Payment was its own puzzle. Deals were settled in a mix of currencies, including the Emirati dirham and the rupee. In May 2023 Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, complained publicly that Russia had piled up billions of rupees in Indian banks that it could not use.

sections.heading: How sanctions actually bite: the plumbing, not the oil
sections.html:
Sanctions sound like a ban on buying something. In practice they are a ban on touching the financial and shipping system that every trade needs. To understand why Indian refiners and banks react so quickly, you need to see the plumbing.

An oil cargo does not just change hands. Someone has to insure the tanker, someone has to finance the purchase with a letter of credit, which is a bank's promise to pay the seller once the oil is delivered, and the payment usually has to pass through banks that deal in dollars. Each of those is a point where Washington or Brussels can apply pressure.

  • Primary sanctions stop a country's own companies and banks from dealing with the target. If the US names a Russian oil company, American banks cannot touch it.
  • Secondary sanctions go further. They threaten anyone in the world who deals with the target with being cut off from the US system. For an Indian bank that clears payments in dollars, that is an existential threat, far bigger than the profit on any single customer.
  • The blacklist, run by the US Treasury, is where named firms, ships and individuals land. Once a company is on it, banks everywhere freeze, insurers walk away and counterparties disappear overnight.

This is why sanctions risk travels so far beyond the sanctioned firm. When the European Union listed Nayara's refinery in July 2025, the company soon had to ask buyers for payment upfront or for documentary letters of credit, because ordinary trade credit dried up. Its chief executive resigned. Nothing about the refinery's steel or pipes had changed; the plumbing around it had.

Russia and its buyers built workarounds: a shadow fleet of older tankers with opaque owners, insurance from outside the West, payment in non-dollar currencies. These work up to a point, but they cost money and they are exactly what the next round of sanctions targets.

sections.heading: The bill arrives: tariffs, oil majors and a refinery in Gujarat
sections.html:
For three years the US tolerated India's Russian purchases, partly because they kept global oil prices from spiking. In 2025 that tolerance ran out, and the pressure came from three directions in quick succession.

First, Europe. In July 2025 the EU's latest sanctions package listed Nayara's Vadinar refinery, the first time an Indian entity had been sanctioned over Russia, along with a ban on importing fuels refined from Russian crude in third countries.

Second, the tariff. In August 2025 the US added a penalty tariff on Indian goods explicitly linked to Russian oil purchases, on top of the reciprocal tariff it had already imposed. That roughly doubled the duty on many Indian exports. The pain fell hardest on labour-intensive sectors that sell heavily to America and compete on thin margins: garments, gems and jewellery, shrimp and seafood, carpets, leather. These are industries where a few points of price decide whether a buyer in New York stays or switches to Vietnam or Bangladesh.

Third, the oil majors. In October 2025 the US Treasury, under Scott Bessent, sanctioned Rosneft and Lukoil, Russia's two largest oil companies, along with dozens of subsidiaries. That made the discounted barrel much harder to buy and finance legally. Reliance said it would recalibrate its Russian purchases to stay compliant, and state refiners began scrutinising every cargo's paperwork.

Then a partial truce. In February 2026, after a call between Donald Trump and Narendra Modi, the US announced a trade deal: a lower reciprocal tariff, and removal of the Russia penalty, with India pledging to stop buying Russian oil. The details stayed thin and talks have since stalled. Meanwhile a new US sanctions law set up a further, heavier round of penalty tariffs on buyers of Russian oil. In mid-October 2026, a day before it was due to take effect, the US paused it, while keeping the right to reimpose it. The risk has been deferred, not removed. And in 2026 American sanctions on Iranian oil trading have named Indian firms too, from traders to shipping managers.

sections.heading: Defence: the dependence that takes decades to unwind
sections.html:
Oil gets the headlines, but the deepest tie between India and Russia is military. A large share of the equipment India's armed forces use today, from fighter jets to tanks to submarines, is of Soviet or Russian origin. Weapons are not like crude oil. You cannot switch suppliers next month, because every aircraft and tank needs spare parts, upgrades and maintenance for decades from the company that built it.

That dependence has shaped Indian diplomacy for half a century, and it explains why India has been careful not to condemn Russia outright. It also creates its own sanctions problem. In 2018 India signed a deal for advanced Russian air-defence systems despite an American law that threatens sanctions on countries buying major Russian weapons. Washington has so far chosen not to apply that law to India, a sign of how much it values the relationship, but the threat remains on the books.

The long-run response has been diversification and domestic production. India now buys more from France, the United States and Israel, and successive governments have pushed to make more weapons at home, with import bans on long lists of items and preference for Indian suppliers in procurement. For investors, this is one of the clearest links between geopolitics and stock prices. Every year that Russian supply looks less reliable, because of sanctions, because Russia needs its output for its own war, or because payment is complicated, the case for Indian defence manufacturers gets stronger.

There is a caution here too. Defence stocks have been re-rated heavily on that story, and much of the order flow is already in the price. The geopolitical tailwind is durable; the valuation is a separate question.

sections.heading: Where it shows up in Indian stocks
sections.html:
Put it all together and the striking thing is how contained the market impact is. Sanctions on Russia have not threatened India's financial system or its growth. They show up in a handful of sectors, each through a specific channel.

  • Refiners. Their crude cost depends on how much discounted Russian oil they can still buy legally, and their export margins depend on whether Europe and others accept their fuel. Each new sanctions round narrows the discount or raises the paperwork.
  • Exporters to the US. Their prices depend on the tariff rate, which since 2025 has been tied in part to India's oil choices. A penalty imposed or removed can swing their competitiveness against Vietnam, Bangladesh and Mexico overnight.
  • Banks. Large Indian banks clear dollars and finance trade. A single deal with a sanctioned name can put their access to the US system at risk, so they tend to be more cautious than the government.
  • Defence. Every strain in the Russian relationship strengthens the case for domestic production.

There is also a link back to the Gulf. If India buys less Russian oil, it buys more from Saudi Arabia, Iraq and the Emirates, which means more of its supply sails through the Strait of Hormuz. With the Iran war disrupting that route in 2026, giving up the Russian barrel has a cost beyond its price. That is the balancing act in one sentence: every relationship India leans on less makes it more dependent on another.

history_title: fifty years of walking between the blocs

history.title: The treaty and the aircraft carrier
history.story:
In August 1971, with East Pakistan in turmoil and millions of refugees pouring into India, Foreign Minister Swaran Singh and his Soviet counterpart Andrei Gromyko signed a treaty of peace, friendship and cooperation in New Delhi. It was not quite an alliance, but it promised that neither would join a military pact against the other.

In December, as India's forces closed in on Dhaka, President Richard Nixon sent a US Navy task force led by the aircraft carrier Enterprise into the Bay of Bengal. The Soviet Union dispatched its own warships, which trailed the Americans in the Indian Ocean. The war ended with the birth of Bangladesh, and a generation of Indian officials never forgot which superpower had sent a carrier.
history.lesson: Defence ties built in a crisis last for decades and are slow to unwind, whatever the oil market does.

history.title: Pokhran and the bonds that beat the sanctions
history.story:
In May 1998 Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee's government conducted nuclear tests at Pokhran. The United States, bound by its own law, imposed sanctions, and Japan and others froze aid and lending. Markets feared India would be cut off from foreign capital just as Asia was in crisis.

Finance minister Yashwant Sinha's answer, announced in his budget that June, was to go to Indians abroad. The State Bank of India launched Resurgent India Bonds for non-resident Indians and raised more than four billion dollars, well above what it had hoped for. Within a few years most sanctions had been lifted.
history.lesson: Sanctions on India have historically been short-lived, and India's diaspora is a financial shock absorber few countries have.

history.title: Cash on the floor of the House
history.story:
Prime Minister Manmohan Singh had staked his government on a civil nuclear deal with the United States that would end India's nuclear isolation. The Left parties, whose support kept the coalition alive, pulled out in protest in July 2008, forcing a confidence vote.

On the day of the vote, three opposition MPs walked up in the Lok Sabha and waved wads of currency notes, alleging they had been offered money to back the government. The scene was broadcast live across the country. The government survived the vote anyway, the deal went through, and India won a waiver from the club of nuclear suppliers later that year.
history.lesson: Over the long run the US relationship has been strategic, not transactional, and Indian governments have paid a high political price to secure it.

history.title: The day the Iran waivers ended
history.story:
When the US reimposed sanctions on Iran in 2018, it gave eight buyers, India among them, temporary waivers to keep importing Iranian oil. In April 2019 the Trump administration said it would not renew them. The goal was to take Iran's oil exports to zero.

India had hoped for an extension. It did not get one. In May 2019 India's ambassador in Washington, Harsh Vardhan Shringla, confirmed that India had stopped buying Iranian oil, adding that it came at a cost because India needed to find other sources of energy.
history.lesson: When the US makes sanctions secondary and means it, Indian refiners comply, whatever the diplomatic rhetoric.

history.title: Less than Europe buys in an afternoon
history.story:
After the invasion of Ukraine, Russian crude went on sale. Indian refiners bought in volume, and within months Russia was India's largest supplier. In April 2022, S. Jaishankar deflected criticism in Washington by pointing out that Europe's Russian energy purchases dwarfed India's. The White House, at the time, publicly defended India's purchases as small.

The arrangement had its oddities. In May 2023, at a regional ministerial meeting in Goa, Sergei Lavrov complained that Russia had accumulated billions of rupees in Indian banks that it could not spend, and needed to convert into another currency.
history.lesson: Geopolitical flexibility can lower India's oil bill, but the gains depend on others tolerating it.

history.title: The bill, the truce and the pause
history.story:
In July 2025 the EU sanctioned Nayara's Gujarat refinery, and its chief executive resigned. In August the US imposed its penalty tariff on Indian goods over Russian oil. In October Scott Bessent's Treasury sanctioned Rosneft and Lukoil, and Reliance said it would recalibrate its purchases. Garment makers and shrimp exporters scrambled to hold on to American buyers.

In February 2026 Donald Trump announced a deal after a call with Narendra Modi: the penalty would go, and India would stop buying Russian oil. Then a new sanctions law threatened a heavier round of penalties on buyers of Russian oil. In mid-October 2026 Washington paused it a day before it took effect, and kept the right to reimpose it.
history.lesson: The discount comes with a bill, and a pause is a deferral, not a settlement.

today:
The heavier round of US penalty tariffs on buyers of Russian oil is on hold, but only on hold: Washington kept the right to reimpose it. US–India trade talks have hit a plateau, and India is reassessing the interim deal while pushing agreements elsewhere, including the free trade deal concluded with the European Union in January 2026. American sanctions on the Iranian oil trade keep naming Indian traders and shipping firms.

The backdrop makes all of this more sensitive. Brent is at [[val:brent]] a barrel and the rupee at [[val:usdinr]] to the dollar, so any loss of cheaper supply hurts more than it would in a calm market. Watch four things: whether the US reimposes the paused penalties; the Russian share of India's crude imports, which shows whether the February pledge is being kept; new Treasury designations involving Indian firms or banks; and the US tariff rate on Indian goods, the number that matters most for exporters.
sowhat:
Sanctions risk is a sector story, not a market story. Size it accordingly.

  • Be careful with refiners whose margins leaned on discounted Russian crude or exports to Europe. Each new sanctions round narrows that edge, and a reimposed penalty would hit them through both crude costs and customer access.
  • Exporters to the US in labour-intensive sectors, garments, gems and jewellery, seafood, carpets, leather, swing with the tariff rate. Treat a penalty removal as a relief rally, not a permanent fix, while the paused round can come back.
  • Banks with large trade-finance and dollar-clearing books carry compliance tail risk. The tell is a new designation that names an Indian counterparty.
  • Prefer domestic defence manufacturers on the structural story, while remembering that much of it is already priced in.
  • Oil-sensitive sectors such as paints, aviation and chemicals lose a cushion if India's crude basket shifts from discounted Russian barrels to full-price Gulf barrels routed through Hormuz.

What would flip it: a durable US–India trade deal with the penalty threat formally withdrawn would lift exporters and ease the pressure on refiners. A reimposition of the paused round, or sanctions on a large Indian bank or refiner, would turn a sector story into a market one.
